catalog_quote: 4.3 Stress Stress in words of Mongolic origin is ultimate in Santa. In other words, stress always falls on the last syllable of any given word. ... When a suffix is added, the stress normally shifts to the last syllable of the word. ... This is the default situation. (462) kuŋ-ˈla 'people' (kuŋ 'person' + -la 'PL') ... However, there is a small set of markers that do not cause the stress to shift when they are added. These are preceded by the symbol '='. ... In addition to these, there are two disyllabic suffixes which only cause the stress to shift to the first syllable of the disyllabic suffix when they are added. ... There are only a couple of words of Mongolic origin which are exceptions to the Santa ultimate stress pattern. (465) 'basi 'tiger' ... 'bosi 'cloth' ... [p.154] In words of Chinese origin the stress pattern is not predictable. ... In summary, stress on words of Mongolic …

audit.reasoning: The coding (fixed final stress in native vocabulary, rightward shift onto suffixes, a listed set of non-shifting clitics and two disyllabic suffixes, lexical exceptions in loans, explicitly weight-blind) rests on a dedicated stress section of the best available grammar (Field 1997, 463-pp UCSB dissertation), which we hold; the quotation was re-verified verbatim against scanned of the held page images at the stated pages (151-154 = PDF 184-187), and the held Nugteren 2011 monograph independently confirms word-final accent for Dongxiang with the same exceptions (ˈbasï, ˈbosï, Arabic and Chinese loans). The one open item fetched sources now (Wu 1994, SPP 55) is silent on stress. Remaining unheld works (Kim 2003 sketch, Liu 1981, Nasunbayar 1981, Todaeva 1961) are older, shorter, or in Chinese/Mongolian/Russian and are unlikely to change the coding; at most Nasunbayar 1981 might add a secondary-stress r
